answerCheck.reason: Interpret the independent random boundary points in the ordinary uniform arclength model. Each side has probability 1/4; vertices have measure zero. Given the first side, the second is the same, adjacent or opposite with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4. For a same-side ordered pair (u, v) in the unit parameter square, |u-v|>=1/2 gives two corner triangles of legs 1/2 and total area 1/4. For adjacent sides, let u, v be distances from their shared corner; distance below 1/2 is the quarter disk u^2+v^2<1/4, of area pi/16. On opposite sides the distance is at least 1, so success is certain. Total probability is (1/4)*(1/4)+(1/2)*(1-pi/16)+1/4=(26-pi)/32, yielding 26+1+32=59. Alternatively keep all 16 ordered side-pair parameter squares as disjoint equal-area pieces: the four same-side squares contribute total favorable area 1, the eight adjacent squares contribute 8-pi/2, and the four opposite squares contribute 4, out of total 16. This gives the same ratio directly, without requiring conditional-probability mastery. Equality-distance boundaries have area zero.

answerCheck.reason: The actual predicates for a truth-teller are (true,false,false), so the answers are YNN. A liar faces(false,false,true) and negates each, giving YYN. For an alternater the predicates are (false,true,false); starting with truth gives NNN, while starting with a lie gives YYY. Therefore only truth-tellers contribute to the difference between the first two yes counts:22-15=7. Each truth-teller receives exactly one candy, so A. All three totals are feasible:7 truth-tellers,6 liars,9 YYY alternaters and 9 NNN alternaters give31 children and yes counts 22,15,9. One method subtracts the count equations T+L+Y=22 and L+Y=15. An optional written calculation subtracts22-15 by borrowing one ten, giving 7; written subtraction is a method choice, not universal evidence of algorithm proficiency.
